After the charter is approved and before setting the schedule or estimating the cost.
Start from the final deliverables stated in the charter, not from activities.
Break each deliverable down into no more than four levels, so that the lowest work package is between 8 and 80 work hours.
Number each element hierarchically (1, 1.1, 1.1.1) and write one tangible output for it.
Assign each work package one owner and an effort estimate in hours.
Check the 100 percent rule: the packages together cover the whole scope with no overlap or excess.
Review the structure with at least one implementer from each package before approving it.
A file in `Docs/` named "Work breakdown structure [project name].md" including a table of code, output, owner and effort.
A structure is not accepted if it has a work package without an owner or an effort estimate, or one that exceeds 80 hours.
A living register that tracks the project's risks, ranks them and assigns an owner to each risk.
At project start, then updated with every status report or when a new risk appears.
Collect the risks in a session of no more than an hour with a representative of each main work package.
Phrase each risk in the form "If [cause] occurs, then [impact] on [objective]".
Rate likelihood and impact on a scale of 1 to 5, and calculate the score by multiplying them.
Rank the risks in descending order, and address every risk with a score of 12 or more with a written response plan.
Assign each risk one owner, the date of the next review and an early indicator that shows it is approaching.
Close the risks whose cause has gone, stating the closing date, and do not delete them.
A file in `Docs/` named "Risk register [project name].md" with columns: number, risk, likelihood, impact, score, response, owner, status.
A register is not accepted if it has a risk with a score of 12 or more without a response plan and a named owner.
A schedule of the main milestones and the completion criteria for each milestone.
After the work breakdown structure is complete and before announcing delivery dates to stakeholders.
Extract from the structure between 5 and 12 milestones that represent completed deliverables, not ongoing activities.
Write for each milestone a completion criterion that can be verified with a yes or no.
Define the due date, the owner and the preceding milestones it depends on.
Add a time buffer of at least 10% between the critical milestones, and state it explicitly.
Mark the milestones tied to an external or contractual commitment with a special flag.
Present the plan to the sponsor and approve the version with a number and a date.
A file in `Docs/` named "Milestone plan [project name].md" including a table of milestone, criterion, date, owner and dependency.
A plan is not accepted if it has a milestone without a verifiable completion criterion, or without a date and an owner.
A brief report that presents the project's position against the plan and calls for the decisions required.
On a fixed day each week throughout the execution period, sent to the sponsor and stakeholders.
Start with an overall status in a single color (green, yellow, red) with the reason for the color in a sentence.
Compare actual progress with the plan in three dimensions: time, cost and scope, in percentages.
State what was completed this week and what will be completed next week in two lists of no more than five items each.
Present the open risks and obstacles from the risk register with the owner of each.
Close with the decisions required from the recipient, each with a deadline.
Keep to one page of no more than 300 words.
A file in `Docs/` named "Status report [project name] week [number].md".
A report is not accepted without a justified color status and numeric variance percentages, or if it exceeds one page.
A structured session that evaluates a completed phase and produces binding improvement actions.
Within a week of closing each phase or main milestone, and before the next phase begins.
Collect the phase data before the session: planned versus actual time, cost and the number of change requests.
Hold a session of no more than 90 minutes with the whole delivery team and without the sponsor present.
Ask each participant for three items: what worked, what stumbled and what must change.
Group the items into themes, and vote to choose the top three themes to address.
Turn each theme into one action with an owner and a date, and do not accept an action without an owner.
Review the previous review's actions and state which were carried out and which were not.
A file in `Docs/QA/` named "Phase review [phase name].md".
A review is not accepted without numeric data for the phase, or if it produces more than three actions or an action without an owner and a date.
A formal form that documents a proposed change to the scope and estimates its impact before it is approved.
When any request arrives that adds to the approved project scope, removes from it or changes its dates.
Write the requested change in one sentence with the requester's name and the request date.
Define the reason for the request and the consequence of rejecting it, and whether it is mandatory or an enhancement.
Estimate the impact in numbers on three dimensions: days added, cost in riyals and work packages affected.
Present at least two options: accept the change in full, accept it partially, or defer it to a later phase.
State the body authorized to approve according to the authority limits in the charter.
Record the final decision in the change log with its number and date, and update the plan if it is approved.
A request is not accepted without a numeric estimate of the impact on time and cost, or without a named approving body.
A closing document that gathers the project's conclusions so they can be used in following projects.
When the project is formally closed, and within two weeks of delivering the last output.
Gather all the phase reviews, the status reports, the risk register and the change log into one source.
Compare the final results with the charter's three indicators and state the variance percentage for each indicator.
Extract between 5 and 10 lessons, and phrase each lesson in the form: the situation, what happened and what should be done in future.
Classify each lesson under one area: scope, time, cost, quality, communication or suppliers.
Interview the sponsor and three stakeholders, for no more than 30 minutes each.
Define for each lesson an actionable recommendation and who adopts it in the next project.
A file in `Docs/` named "Lessons learned [project name].md".
A document is not accepted without a numeric comparison with the charter's indicators, or if it has a lesson without a recommendation and a specific area.
Handling a customer complaint from receipt to closure with a documented reply and a corrective action.
When a customer complaint arrives that goes beyond an immediate fix and needs investigation and a written reply.
Record the complaint in one line: the customer, the channel, the date, the product or service, and the severity classification (low, medium, high).
Send the acknowledgment within 4 working hours, and state in it the date of the final reply, no later than 3 working days.
Collect the facts from the records and the parties concerned, and distinguish between what is proven and what is alleged.
Identify the direct cause and the root cause, and propose compensation or a correction proportionate to the severity.
Write the reply to the customer: a specific apology, what happened, what will be done, the date of implementation and the follow-up contact.
Close the complaint after the customer confirms or after 5 working days from the reply without objection, and record the lesson learned.
Handling is not accepted without a written root cause, a reply documented with its date and a corrective action that has an owner and a date.
Drafting a service level agreement with measurable indicators and clear limits of commitment.
When defining support commitments toward a customer or an internal department before the service begins or when it is renewed.
Define the scope of the service in one paragraph, and what is explicitly outside the scope.
Classify requests into four priority levels, and for each level: first response time, resolution time and coverage hours.
Define at least three indicators: the rate of meeting the resolution time, the first-contact resolution rate and customer satisfaction, with a numeric target for each indicator.
Write the measurement mechanism: the data source, the reporting frequency (monthly) and who reviews it.
Define the consequences of a breach and the exceptions (external outages, force majeure) and the escalation mechanism.
Add a schedule for reviewing the agreement every 6 months and the names of the signatories.
A file in `Docs/` named "Service level agreement [service].md".
An agreement is not accepted if it has an indicator without a numeric target or a priority level without a defined resolution time.
Building a frequently asked questions page from actual ticket data with short, up-to-date answers.
When the same questions recur in the support channels or before launching a new product or service.
Extract the tickets of the last 90 days and classify them by topic, and choose every topic that recurred 10 times or more.
Phrase each question as the customer asks it, in their words, not in the team's terms.
Write each answer in 3 lines at most, starting directly with the solution, then the condition or exception if any.
Arrange the questions in groups of no more than 7 questions each, the most frequent first.
Present the draft to two members of the support team to verify accuracy, and to one customer to test clarity.
Fix the review date and an update schedule every 3 months.
A page is not accepted if it has a question that did not appear in the tickets, an answer that exceeds 3 lines or no review date.
Turning customers' written feedback into themes ranked by frequency and impact, with recommendations.
When customer feedback from surveys, reviews and tickets piles up without systematic analysis.
Gather the feedback in one table with columns: source, date, text and rating if available, with a minimum of 100 items of feedback.
Classify each item under one theme and one sentiment (positive, negative, neutral), using a list of no more than 12 themes.
Calculate for each theme: frequency, the share of negative feedback and the trend compared with the previous period.
Choose the top 5 themes by negative impact, and attach two verbatim quotations to each theme.
Write for each theme one actionable recommendation and a proposed owner.
A file in `Outputs/` named "Customer feedback analysis [period].md" with the data table in `Data/`.
An analysis is not accepted without a source table, without a numeric frequency for each theme and without a verbatim quotation supporting each conclusion.
Defining the escalation levels, their owners and their timings for unresolved support cases.
When cases are resolved late because there is no declared escalation path or when several parties are responsible.
Define three escalation levels: first line, supervisor and management, and for each level the name of the owner and a backup.
Define the escalation condition for each level: exceeding the resolution time, the severity of the case or the customer's explicit request.
Fix the time to move between levels: 4 working hours for the second level and 8 hours for the third level.
Write the escalation channel and the mandatory content of the message: case number, customer, previous attempts and what is requested.
Add the immediate escalation cases that bypass the levels (a complete service outage, a legal risk).
Test the matrix on 5 past cases and adjust it according to the results.
A matrix is not accepted if it has a level without a named owner and backup or without a transition time defined in hours.
Analyzing the customers lost in a given period and identifying the causes that can be addressed.
When the cancellation or stop-buying rate rises above the expected limit or at the quarterly review.
Define a lost customer numerically (a subscription cancellation or a 90-day purchase gap) and calculate the monthly rate for the last 6 months.
Extract the list of lost customers with columns: join date, loss date, monthly value, number of complaints and last interaction.
Divide the lost customers into segments by tenure and value, and identify the segment with the highest loss.
Contact at least 10 lost customers from the highest-loss segment and extract the main reason for each of them.
Classify the reasons into addressable and not addressable, and calculate the value at risk for each reason.
Propose two retention actions for the top two addressable reasons, with a success indicator and a measurement date.
A file in `Outputs/` named "Churn review [period].md" with the list of lost customers in `Data/`.
A review is not accepted without a documented monthly loss rate, without at least 10 interviews and without a financial value for each reason.
Designing a customer satisfaction survey after service, running it and analyzing its results.
When customer satisfaction needs to be measured after dealing with support or after delivering a service.
Define the measurement goal and its indicator: customer satisfaction CSAT out of 5, or Net Promoter Score NPS out of 10, and do not combine the two in one survey.
Write 5 questions at most: the indicator question first, then one open question about the reason, then the sub-aspect questions.
Send the survey within 24 hours of closing the case, and aim for a sample size of at least 100 responses or 30% of cases.
Test the survey on 5 customers before launch and adjust any question that was understood in more than one way.
Analyze the results by channel, employee and case type, and classify the open answers into themes.
Write 3 main findings and one action for the lowest-rated aspect.
A file in `Outputs/` named "Satisfaction survey [service] [period].md" with the raw responses in `Data/`.
A survey is not accepted if it exceeds 5 questions, nor is a report on a sample under 100 responses without a written justification.
Preparing uniform reply templates for the most frequent support cases with mandatory personalization fields.
When the quality of replies varies between support staff or when the same replies are repeatedly written by hand.
Choose the top 15 cases by frequency from the tickets of the last 60 days, and give each case a name and a unique code.
Write for each case a template of 4 parts: a greeting with the customer's name, an acknowledgment of the problem, the solution or next step, and a closing with the follow-up contact.
Put the personalization fields in square brackets such as [customer name] and [order number], and do not send the template before filling them all in.
Keep to a limit of 120 words per template, and to a single formal tone that does not change between templates.
Review the templates with the support supervisor and the brand officer, and approve them with a date and a version.
Assign an owner for the templates and a review schedule every 3 months or when the policy changes.
A file in `Docs/` named "Support reply templates [channel].md".
A template is not accepted if it exceeds 120 words, lacks a [customer name] field or has no version number and approval date.
Writing a documented prompt for a language model with inputs, outputs and testable constraints.
When a prompt is needed that will be reused with a language model, not a prompt written once and forgotten.
Write the prompt's goal in one sentence, and identify the user who runs it and the context it works in.
Define the required inputs one by one: each input's name, its type, whether it is mandatory, and one example of it.
Define the output form precisely: the format (text, table, JSON), the maximum length, the language and the mandatory fields.
Write the explicit constraints: what the model is forbidden to do, and how it behaves when inputs are missing or conflicting.
Attach at least three test cases: an input, an expected output, and at least one of them an edge case.
Run the prompt on the three cases and record the result; adjust the wording until all the cases pass.
A specification is not accepted without a defined output form and three documented passing test cases.
Building a set of test cases for an AI agent and measuring its success rate before approval.
Before approving an AI agent in real work, or after any substantial change to its instructions or tools.
Write the task the agent is measured on in one sentence, and the success criterion for each case (correctness of the output, adherence to the format, or execution time).
Build at least twenty test cases: half of them ordinary cases, a quarter edge cases, and a quarter incomplete or misleading inputs.
Fix for each case: the input, the acceptable output and the forbidden behavior (such as fabricating data or carrying out an action without permission).
Run the agent on all the cases three times to detect variability, and record the results in a table with columns: case number, result, reason for failure.
Calculate the overall success rate and the success rate on the edge cases separately, and classify the failure reasons into three categories at most.
Write the recommendation: approve, approve conditionally with human supervision, or redesign, with the three most impactful failure cases.
A file in `Docs/QA/` named "Agent evaluation [topic].md" with the cases table in `Data/`.
An evaluation is not accepted with fewer than twenty test cases, or without a separate success rate for the edge cases.
Determining whether a manual procedure deserves automation, with which tool and at what return.
When proposing to automate a repeated manual procedure before spending any effort building it.
Describe the current procedure in five steps at most, with its monthly frequency and the time taken in each run.
Calculate the current annual cost: number of runs × time × hourly cost, and add the cost of the errors recorded in the last three months.
Rate the automation suitability in a table with three criteria from 1 to 5: stability of the rules, structure of the inputs and few exceptions; a procedure with a total below 10 is not nominated.
Identify the most suitable tool (a no-code automation tool, a script, or an agent using a language model) with the reason for choosing it and for excluding the other two.
Estimate the build cost and the annual maintenance, and calculate the payback period in months.
Write the decision: nominate, defer or exclude, with the next step and its owner.
A nomination is not accepted without a calculated current annual cost and a payback period in months.
Drawing a complete workflow with its steps, owners and handoff points to reveal delay and repetition.
When analyzing a workflow that passes through more than one person or system and has no documented diagram.
Define the start event and the end event of the workflow in one sentence each.
Gather the steps from at least three people who actually perform them, not from the official procedure description.
Record each step in a table with columns: number, description, performer, system used, execution time, waiting time before it.
Draw the map in Mermaid format, and distinguish the handoff points between people or systems with a different color or shape.
Calculate the total time and the total waiting time, and flag every step whose wait is longer than a working day or that recurs twice.
Choose three improvement points at most, ranked by their impact on the total time.
A file in `Docs/` named "Workflow map [topic].md" containing the diagram and the table.
A map is not accepted without a recorded waiting time for every step or without distinguished handoff points in the diagram.
A structured check of the risks of introducing an AI model into a task before running it.
Before running an AI model in a task that touches real data or decisions that affect people.
Describe the proposed use in two sentences: what the user enters and what the system does with the output.
Classify the data handled: public, internal, personal or confidential; and determine whether it is sent to an external provider.
Assess five risks in a table: fabrication of information, data leakage, bias, over-reliance and lack of accountability; for each risk a likelihood and an impact from 1 to 5.
For each risk whose score (likelihood × impact) is 12 or more, write a specific mitigation action and an owner for it.
Identify the decisions in which relying on the output without documented human review is forbidden.
Write the final verdict: permitted, permitted with conditions or prohibited, with a re-check date.
A file in `Docs/QA/` named "AI risk check [topic].md".
A check is not accepted without a data classification and a table of the five risks with their scores and mitigation actions.
Preparing a labeling guide that keeps annotators consistent when labeling data to train or evaluate a model.
When data needs to be labeled by more than one person, or by a model followed by human review.
Write the purpose of the labeling and how it will be used in one sentence, and define the unit of labeling (a line, a message or an image).
Define each category with an explicit definition, two positive examples and a nearby negative example that is easy to confuse with it.
Write tie-breaking rules for ambiguous cases, and add an "undetermined" category with the conditions for using it.
Choose a pilot sample of 50 items and label it with two independent annotators, and calculate the agreement rate between them.
Review every disagreement, and adjust the definitions until the agreement rate reaches 85% or more before starting the full labeling.
Fix the format of the labeling file: columns for the identifier, the text or reference, the category, the annotator and the date.
A file in `Docs/` named "Labeling guide [topic].md" with the pilot sample in `Data/`.
A guide is not accepted without a documented pilot sample and an agreement rate between annotators of at least 85%.
Identifying where an automated system must stop for human review and how.
When designing an automated procedure or an agent that makes decisions or carries out actions whose effect is not easily reversed.
Write all the steps of the automated procedure in a numbered list, and flag every step that produces a decision or carries out an action outside the system.
Classify each flagged step by reversibility: reversible within minutes, reversible at a cost, or irreversible.
Place a mandatory intervention point at every step that is irreversible, exceeds a declared financial limit or touches personal data.
Define for each point: who reviews, what they see, the maximum response deadline, and what happens when it passes without a response.
Write the automatic escalation conditions: a confidence level below 80%, or cases outside the known examples.
Record every human intervention in a log with columns: date, step, decision, reviewer, reason; and review it monthly to reduce the excess points.
A file in `Docs/` named "Human intervention points [procedure].md".
A design is not accepted if it has an irreversible step without a human intervention point with a defined reviewer and deadline.
Documenting an AI model in use: its purpose, data, performance and limits on one page.
When adopting an AI model in work or handing it to another team without prior documentation.
Record the model's identity: the name, the version, the provider, the adoption date and the internal owner responsible for it.
Write the approved purpose in one sentence, and a list of at least three prohibited uses.
Describe the data: the source of the training or tuning data if known, and the scope of the data it was tested on internally.
Record the performance in a table: the measure, the value, a test sample size of at least 100 items, and the measurement date.
Write the known limits: the languages or categories where it is weak, and the recurring error patterns observed.
Define the periodic review date (every six months at most) and the conditions for withdrawing approval.
A file in `Docs/` named "Model card [model name].md".
A card is not accepted without a performance table on a sample of at least 100 items and a list of prohibited uses.
Building a short checklist that judges a deliverable before it is handed over.
When there is a recurring deliverable handed to another party and the same errors repeat.
Collect the last 10 cases of the deliverable, and record every comment or return that came back on them.
Turn the comments into check items of no more than 12, each item a question answered with yes or no.
Arrange the items in the natural order of checking: completeness, then correctness, then wording and formatting.
Define for each item: who checks it, what evidence is acceptable, and whether the item is critical and stops delivery or secondary.
Try the list on 3 past cases, and delete every item that did not catch a single error.
Put the version number, its date and its owner at the head of the list.
A list is not accepted if it exceeds 12 items or contains an item that cannot be answered with yes or no.
Root cause analysis of a quality defect
Tracing a quality defect or a safety incident to its root cause with evidence, not guesswork.
When a quality defect or a safety incident recurs more than twice in a single month despite the immediate fix.
Describe the defect in one sentence with numbers: what happened, where, when, how many times and what it cost.
Gather the evidence before the analysis: the records, the photos and the statements of at least two people who handled the case.
Ask "why" five times in a row, and support each answer with written evidence or record it as a hypothesis.
Classify the causes on four axes: people, method, equipment and materials, and judge each cause by evidence.
Choose the one root cause which, if removed, would stop the defect recurring, and write why the alternatives were excluded.
Define the removal action, its owner and the verification date after 30 days.
An analysis is not accepted if it stops at a human cause or contains a "why" without evidence or a declared hypothesis.
Documenting a repeated task as a step-by-step procedure that a new employee can carry out without asking.
When a task recurs at least weekly and its execution differs depending on who performs it.
Observe the actual execution twice with two different people, and record every difference between them.
Write the goal, scope and owner in three lines at the head of the procedure.
Divide the task into steps of no more than 15, each step one imperative verb with one actor.
Add at each critical step: the check point, the acceptable value and what to do on failure.
Attach the tools and forms required with their paths, and set a time limit for the whole procedure.
Hand the procedure to someone who has never performed the task, and amend it until they carry it out without a single question.
A procedure is not accepted if it has not been tried on a new performer or contains a step with more than one actor.
Carrying out a field inspection round with a fixed checklist and documenting violations by severity.
Periodically every week at an operating site, or immediately after an incident or a change in equipment.
Define the round's route and zones, and do not exceed 8 zones in a single round.
Use a fixed checklist for each zone: exits, fire, electricity, hazardous materials and protective equipment.
Document each violation with a photo, an exact location and a severity level: high is addressed within 24 hours, medium within 7 days, low within 30 days.
Stop any work at a high-severity violation before completing the round.
Assign an owner and a date for each violation, and close the previous round's violations by field verification, not by declaration.
A round report is not accepted if it has a violation without a photo, a severity level, an owner or a closing date.
Drafting a corrective action that removes the cause of a nonconformity and whose effect is verified.
When there is a documented nonconformity from an audit, a customer complaint or a recurring defect after its cause has been analyzed.
Write the nonconformity in one sentence with its reference: the audit or complaint number and its date.
Distinguish between the immediate treatment of the case and the corrective action for the cause, and write both.
Define the corrective action: what changes, who carries it out, and by what date, no later than 30 days.
Set a numeric verification indicator: the number of recurrences in the 60 days after implementation compared with the previous period.
Review after the date: close the action if recurrence falls to zero, otherwise re-analyze the cause.
A corrective action is not accepted without a defined root cause, a numeric verification indicator and a review date.
Verifying that a documented procedure is actually carried out as written, and documenting the gaps.
Periodically every quarter for each critical procedure, or when there is doubt that execution contradicts the document.
Read the documented procedure and extract verifiable check points, no fewer than 5 points.
Choose a random sample of 10 cases executed in the last 90 days, and check each case's record.
Interview at least two performers, and ask them to demonstrate the execution, not describe it.
Record each gap with a classification: a violation of the document, a gap in the document, or a better undocumented practice.
Calculate the conformity rate: the conforming cases over the sample, and write the findings ordered by impact.
Hand the report to the procedure owner, and request a closure plan within 14 days.
An audit is not accepted with a sample of fewer than 10 cases or with a finding without documented evidence and a case reference.
Defining the conditions for accepting a deliverable or a handover in a checkable form before work begins.
Before starting any work that is handed to another party, or when there is a recurring dispute over whether a handover is complete.
Write the required deliverable in one sentence, and who accepts it by name, not by title.
Write from 3 to 8 criteria, each criterion starting with a checking verb: "contains", "does not exceed", "matches", "works when".
Give each criterion a measurable value: a number, a percentage, a duration or a reference to compare against.
Classify the criteria into mandatory ones, without which it is rejected, and desirable ones, which are recorded as a comment.
Present the criteria to the accepting party, and approve them by signature or message before work begins.
Criteria are not accepted if any of them contains an unmeasured description such as "good", "suitable" or "clear".
Organizing a workplace with the five-step method and fixing the order with a written standard.
At a workplace where more than 10 minutes a day are wasted searching for tools or materials.
Sort: put a red tag on every item not used within 30 days, and remove it from the site within a week.
Set in order: assign each remaining item a fixed, marked place, so that reaching it takes no more than 30 seconds.
Shine: clean the whole site, and record every fault or damage discovered during cleaning.
Standardize: photograph the standard condition, and post the photo and the daily list to maintain it at the site.
Sustain: carry out a weekly check of five items, and record the result out of 25 points in a visible log.
An implementation is not accepted without a photo of the standard condition and a weekly check log with a recorded score.
Carrying out a physical inventory count, reconciling it with the records and documenting the differences.
When closing an accounting period, or when differences are suspected between the book balance and the actual balance.
Freeze inventory movement before counting begins, and export the book balance for each item with the columns: code, name, unit, book quantity, location.
Divide the locations into count zones, and assign each zone a counter and an independent reviewer who does not see the other's result.
Recount every item whose difference exceeds 2% of the book balance or 500 riyals in value before approving the result.
Record the final differences in a table with the columns: item, book, actual, difference, value, probable reason.
Classify the reasons for the differences into defined categories: damage, recording error, theft, counting error, then propose a corrective action for each category.
Submit the adjustment entry for approval with the list of items that need more frequent cycle counting.
A file in `Docs/` named "Inventory report [site] [period].md" with the differences sheet in `Data/`.
An inventory report is not accepted without a double count of the items with differences, or with differences whose reason is not classified.
Building a quantitative demand forecast from historical data and measuring its accuracy.
When planning procurement, operating capacity or the budget for an upcoming period based on past sales or consumption data.
Gather a time series of at least 24 consecutive periods with the columns: date, item or category, quantity, and flag the outlier periods such as seasons and closures.
Calculate the three-period moving average, the annual growth, and the seasonality factor for each period from at least last year's data.
Build at least two models, one of them simple for comparison, and hold back the last 6 periods for testing without including them in the build.
Measure accuracy on the test periods with the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), and exclude any model whose error exceeds 20%.
Present the forecast in three scenarios: base, optimistic and conservative, with each scenario's assumption in one line.
Set the next review date and who owns updating the model when new data arrives.
A file in `Outputs/` named "Demand forecast [item] [period].md" with the forecast table in `Data/`.
A forecast is not accepted without an accuracy measure calculated on independent test periods, or without three scenarios with declared assumptions.
A periodic review of open sales opportunities, cleaning them up and estimating the expected closings.
Weekly with the sales team, or before preparing the revenue forecast for an upcoming period.
Export the open opportunities with the columns: customer, value, stage, creation date, last activity date, expected close date, owner.
Flag every opportunity with no activity recorded for 30 days or whose expected close date has passed, and ask for a decision on it: update or close.
Check that the stage is consistent with the evidence: no opportunity stays in the "negotiation" stage without a documented quote, nor in "qualified" without a known budget and decision maker.
Calculate the weighted value of each stage using the team's historical close rate, not the owner's estimate, and compare it with the quarter's target.
Identify the 5 largest opportunities by value, and for each: the current obstacle, the next step, its date and who owns it.
Record the opportunities closed this week with the loss reason from a defined list, not free text.
A review is not accepted if it leaves an opportunity without activity for more than 30 days without a decision, or calculates the weighted value from a personal estimate.
Tracking the behavior of customer groups by their join date to measure retention and value.
When you need to know whether customer retention is improving or declining over time, or to measure the effect of a change in the product or pricing.
Define the cohort by the date of the customer's first transaction, grouped monthly, and define the return event precisely in one sentence, such as "a paid purchase".
Prepare a table with the columns: customer identifier, join month, activity month, and make sure every cohort has at least 50 customers; otherwise merge it with the adjacent cohort.
Build the retention matrix: the rows are cohorts, the columns are months 1 to 12 after joining, and the values are the share of active customers.
Compare the cohorts at fixed points: month 1, month 3 and month 6, and flag any cohort that deviates from the average of the previous cohorts by more than 5 percentage points.
Tie each notable deviation to a documented event with its date, such as a campaign, a price change or an outage, or state explicitly that the cause is unknown.
Close with three actionable findings at most, each naming the cohort it rests on.
A file in `Outputs/` named "Cohort analysis [product] [period].md" with the retention matrix in `Data/`.
An analysis is not accepted with a cohort of fewer than 50 customers, or with a notable deviation that was neither tied to an event nor declared to have an unknown cause.
Writing a complete dashboard specification before building it: the indicators, sources, refresh and permissions.
Before building any data analysis dashboard, or when a substantial change to an existing dashboard is requested.
Define the audience and the decision the dashboard serves in one sentence, and limit the main indicators to 6 at most on the first page.
Write for each indicator: the name, the formula, the unit, the source, the data table and its column, the desired direction and the alert threshold.
Define the data sources and the refresh pattern for each source: daily, weekly or real time, and who is responsible for its quality.
Sketch the page layout: the first page for the summary, a page for each analysis axis, with the shared filters.
Define the permissions: who sees each page, and which rows are restricted by user.
Write the list of acceptance tests: reconcile each indicator with the original source for a sample of 3 periods, and a load time of no more than 5 seconds.
A specification is not accepted with an indicator that has no defined formula and source, or with more than 6 main indicators on the first page.
A systematic check of a dataset before using it in an analysis or a report.
When a new dataset is received, or before relying on data in a decision or an executive report.
Document the source, the extraction date and the number of rows and columns, and compare the row count with what is expected from the original system.
Check each column on six dimensions: completeness, uniqueness, type, range, consistency and timeliness, and record the result in a table.
Flag every column in which the share of missing values exceeds 5%, every duplicate key, and every value outside its logical range such as a future date or a negative quantity.
Choose a random sample of 30 rows and reconcile it manually with the original source, and record the number of rows that match.
Classify each problem: critical and blocks use, medium and needs correction, or low and only documented, with the proposed action and its owner.
Write a final verdict in one line: fit for use, fit with conditions, or unfit.
A check is not accepted without a sample reconciliation against the original source, or without an explicit final verdict on the fitness of the data.
Preparing a uniform request for quotations to suppliers and comparing the offers against announced criteria.
When a purchase exceeds the direct authority limit, or when renewing a supply contract that requires competition.
Write the technical specification of what is required: quantities, specifications, delivery place and date, payment terms and the offer's validity period.
Announce the evaluation criteria and their weights before sending, for example: price 50%, quality 25%, delivery time 15% and warranty 10%.
Send the request to at least 3 qualified suppliers on the same day, with a uniform response form that ensures comparability.
Set a single deadline for receiving offers, and reject any offer that arrives after it or departs from the response form.
Compare the offers in a table against the announced criteria, and exclude any offer more than 25% below the average of the offers unless there is a documented justification.
Write the award recommendation at the start of the memo with its decisive reason, and who approves it.
A file in `Docs/Decisions/` named "Request for quotations [item].md" with the comparison table in `Data/`.
A request is not accepted with fewer than 3 suppliers, or with evaluation criteria that were not announced before the offers were received.
Matching supplier invoices to purchase orders and goods receipts before payment.
Before approving any payment to a supplier, or at month close to account for unpaid obligations.
Gather the received invoices in a table with the columns: invoice number, supplier, date, amount, purchase order number, goods receipt number.
Match each invoice to the purchase order and the goods receipt on three dimensions: item, quantity and unit price.
Automatically accept invoices whose difference does not exceed 1% of the purchase order value or 100 riyals, whichever is lower, and hold the rest.
Check for duplicates by matching the supplier, the amount and the date within 30 days, and hold any invoice without a prior purchase order.
Record the held invoices in a table with the columns: invoice, type of difference, amount, who is responsible for resolving it, due date.
Issue the approved payment list with the total amount and the number of invoices, and a summary of the held items by type of difference.
A file in `Docs/` named "Invoice matching [supplier or period].md" with the matching table in `Data/`.
A payment list is not accepted if it includes an invoice without a three-way match, or a held invoice without a resolution owner and date.
Preparing a brief board presentation that opens with the decision required and condenses the evidence.
When presenting results or requesting approval before the board of directors or a senior committee in limited time.
On the first slide, write the decision or message required in one sentence, and exactly what is asked of the board.
Define three main indicators and no more, each with: the current value, the target and the trend compared with the previous period.
Present the top three risks with their likelihood, their impact and the mitigation action for each.
Dedicate one slide to the options and one slide to the recommendation, and the presentation does not exceed twelve slides.
Move the detailed tables and the methodology to a separate appendix that is shown only when asked.
Write for each slide a title that carries its conclusion in a complete sentence, not a descriptive title.
A file in `Outputs/` named "Board presentation [topic].md" containing the slide outline and the appendix.
A presentation is not accepted if it does not announce the decision required on its first slide or exceeds twelve slides before the appendix.
Writing meeting minutes that record the decisions, tasks, owners and dates.
After any meeting in which decisions were taken or tasks were distributed that need follow-up.
In the header write: the meeting topic, its date, the attendees, those who sent apologies, and who took the minutes.
Record the decisions taken in a table with the columns: decision number, decision text, and who approved it.
Record the tasks in a table with the columns: the task, the owner by a single name, and the due date as a specific date.
Record the deferred points and the unresolved disagreements in a separate section with who owns resolving them.
Send the minutes to the attendees within twenty-four hours, and request corrections within a window of two working days.
Minutes are not accepted if they contain a task without a single named owner and a specific due date.
Drafting a business proposal for the client that ties their problem to the solution, scope, price and schedule.
When approaching a client or an organization with a service or a project that needs written agreement on the scope and cost.
On the first page, write your understanding of the client's problem in three sentences, and the result they are buying, not the service you sell.
Define the scope in two lists: what the proposal includes, and what it explicitly does not include.
Divide the execution into no more than five phases, and for each phase: the outputs, the duration and the completion criterion.
Present the price in a single table with the payment terms and the proposal's validity period as a specific date.
Add the assumptions the price rests on, and what the proposal requires of the client in data or approvals.
Close with the acceptance step: who signs, and what happens in the first week after signing.
A file in `Docs/` named "Business proposal [client name].md".
A proposal is not accepted without an explicit list of exclusions or without an expiry date for the price's validity.
Preparing an urgent statement in a crisis that establishes the facts, defines the action and states the update channel.
When an incident occurs that touches customers, reputation or operations and calls for a public response within hours.
Gather only the confirmed facts in a list, and separate them from the unconfirmed estimates, which are not published.
Write the statement in four paragraphs: what happened, who was affected, what we have done, and what comes next and when.
Keep to no more than two hundred words, and do not state a cause that has not been established or a responsibility that has not been settled.
Name the single official spokesperson, the updates channel, and the time of the next update at a specific hour.
Prepare a list of five expected questions from the media or customers and a uniform answer for each.
Present the statement to the legal function and the decision maker before publishing, and document who approved it and when.
A file in `Docs/` named "Crisis statement [topic] [date].md" containing the statement and the list of questions.
A statement is not accepted if it includes an unconfirmed fact or lacks the next update time and the spokesperson's name.
Building the outline of a speech or an address around a single message with a calculated time and clear transition points.
When preparing to deliver a speech at an event, an opening or a formal session with a time set in advance.
Write the one message the audience must leave with in a sentence of no more than fifteen words.
Define the speech's duration in minutes, and distribute it across: an opening of no more than ten percent, three main points and a conclusion.
For each main point write: the idea, one piece of evidence or a short story, and a transition sentence to the next point.
Calculate the word count on the basis of one hundred and thirty words per minute, and cut whatever exceeds the time.
Write the opening sentence and the closing sentence out in full, and make the close a call to a specific action.
An outline is not accepted without a single declared message at its start, or if its word count exceeds the set time.
Preparing an issue of a periodic newsletter with fixed sections, brief content and a single call to action.
When issuing a periodic issue for an internal or external audience on a fixed weekly or monthly schedule.
Fix the newsletter's sections in a template that does not change between issues, with no more than five sections.
Write the issue title in under fifty characters, and an introductory line that states its most important news.
Write for each section a paragraph of no more than eighty words and one link for details when needed.
Place a single call to action in the whole issue, in a prominent position, in a clear imperative form.
Check the names, numbers and dates against their source before sending, and record the send date and the open rate in the issues log.
An issue is not accepted if it includes more than one call to action or any section in it exceeds eighty words.
Drafting an internal policy with a scope, definitions, rules, responsibilities and an exception path.
When a recurring behavior or practice inside the organization needs to be governed by a binding, approved rule.
Write the purpose of the policy in one sentence, and its scope: whom it covers, and what it explicitly excludes.
Define the key terms in a table before the rules, with no more than ten of them.
Write the rules numbered, each rule a single binding sentence in the form "must" or "is prohibited", not a recommendation.
Define for each rule the implementation owner, the oversight owner and the consequence of a violation.
Add the exception request path: who requests, who approves, and the maximum response time in working days.
Fix the version number, the effective date and the periodic review date, no more than twelve months out.
A policy is not accepted if it has a rule phrased as a recommendation, or without an implementation owner, or without an exception path.
Writing a delegation brief that defines the required result, the limits of authority and the follow-up points.
When assigning a task or a responsibility to another person that lasts longer than a day or requires decisions in your name.

Define the limits of authority: what the delegate decides alone, what comes back to you before execution, and the spending cap if any.
State the available resources: files, contacts, tools and who to consult when stuck.
Define the follow-up points with fixed dates, no more than three, and what is presented at each point.
Ask the delegate to restate the task in their own words in a paragraph before starting, and approve it or correct it.
A delegation is not accepted without a measurable success criterion or without limits of authority written explicitly.

Pasos
Define el procedimiento por sus límites: dónde empieza y dónde termina.
Elige como máximo tres medidas: tiempo, errores, y coste o esfuerzo.
Mide el estado actual en una muestra de al menos cinco casos y registra el método de medición.
Realiza la mejora y luego mide de la misma manera en una muestra comparable.
Expresa la diferencia como cifra y como porcentaje, y di con claridad que lo que no pudiste medir queda sin medir.
Una tabla en `Data/` llamada «Medición [procedimiento].csv»: medida, antes, después, diferencia, método de medición.
Criterio de aceptación
No se acepta una afirmación de mejora sin dos cifras comparables tomadas de la misma manera.
Informe ejecutivo
Un informe breve que empieza por la conclusión y que quien decide puede leer en dos minutos.
Estructura
La conclusión en tres líneas: la situación, la decisión requerida y el impacto.
Las tres cifras más importantes en una tabla.
Qué se completó, qué se retrasó y por qué.
Las decisiones requeridas, numeradas, cada una con una recomendación y una fecha.
Riesgos en tres líneas como máximo.
Una página. Sin relleno ni preámbulo. Cada cifra tiene una fuente, indicada entre paréntesis. Se guarda en `Docs/Reports/`.
Revisión de calidad
Comprobar un entregable y juzgarlo como aprobado o rechazado.
Lee la tarea del tablero y el criterio de aceptación antes de leer el entregable.
Comprueba el entregable por orden: primero que esté completo respecto a lo pedido, luego la corrección del contenido y por último la forma y el lenguaje.
Registra cada comentario con su ubicación exacta, su motivo y lo que lo corregiría.
El veredicto: «aprobado» o «rechazado» con un motivo decisivo. «Aprobado con comentarios» existe solo para la forma.
Un archivo en `Docs/QA/` llamado «Revisión de la fila [número].md» y una actualización del estado de la fila.
Análisis de causa raíz
Llegar a la causa de un problema recurrente en lugar de tratar sus síntomas.
Describe el problema con hechos: qué, cuándo, cuántas veces y su impacto.
Pregunta «por qué» cinco veces seguidas y escribe cada respuesta con su evidencia.
Clasifica las causas: personas, procedimiento, herramientas y datos.
Elige la causa que, una vez eliminada, hace desaparecer el problema, y verifícala con al menos un caso.
Propón una acción preventiva, no correctiva.
Una página en `Outputs/` con el árbol de causas, la acción propuesta y la forma de verificarla.
Mapeo de procesos
Documentar un procedimiento actual con sus pasos, responsables y duración.
Operaciones
Define la entrada con la que empieza el procedimiento y la salida con la que termina.
Escribe los pasos, numerados, y para cada paso: quién lo realiza, qué necesita, cuánto tarda y dónde espera.
Marca los puntos de espera, repetición y aprobaciones.
Propón la versión objetivo eliminando un paso, fusionando dos o automatizando uno.
Una tabla de pasos en `Outputs/` en formato Markdown, que luego pueda dibujarse como diagrama.
Diseño de un agente para un procedimiento
Convertir un procedimiento repetido en un agente de IA controlado.
Elige un procedimiento repetido con entradas claras y una salida que pueda verificarse.
Escribe para el agente: el objetivo, las entradas, la salida, lo que tiene prohibido hacer y cuándo se detiene y pregunta.
Define el punto de revisión humana antes de cualquier efecto externo.
Pruébalo con cinco casos reales con los datos identificativos enmascarados y registra el resultado de cada caso.
Aplica la habilidad «Medición antes y después».
El archivo de descripción del agente en `Outputs/` y la tabla de pruebas en `Data/`.
Redacción de una política o procedimiento
Redactar una política o una guía de procedimiento de forma vinculante y clara.
Propósito y alcance en dos líneas.
Definiciones, si hacen falta.
Reglas, numeradas, con «debe» y «no debe», no consejos.
Roles y responsabilidades en una tabla.
Excepciones y quién las aprueba.
Revisión periódica y responsable del documento.
Una frase por regla. Sin sinónimos para un mismo término. Lo que no tiene responsable no se escribe.
Preparación de una presentación
Construir una historia persuasiva antes de diseñar las diapositivas.
Presentación y persuasión
Escribe el único mensaje con el que debe quedarse la audiencia.
Construye la historia: la situación, el problema, la solución, la evidencia y la petición.
Cada diapositiva tiene un título que enuncia la conclusión, no el tema.
Como máximo una cifra destacada por diapositiva.
La última diapositiva: la decisión requerida y el siguiente paso.
El esquema de diapositivas como texto en `Outputs/` antes de cualquier diseño.
Análisis de datos
Analizar un archivo de datos y llegar a conclusiones fiables.
Datos
Entiende las columnas, su origen y sus unidades antes de cualquier cálculo.
Comprueba la calidad: vacíos, duplicados y valores atípicos, y anota lo que encuentres.
Responde solo a la pregunta concreta de la tarea, con tres cifras clave.
Para cada cifra: cómo se calculó y los filtros aplicados.
Di que lo que los datos no respaldan no puede afirmarse.
Un resumen en `Outputs/` y la tabla de resultados en `Data/` en formato CSV.
Diseño de un panel de indicadores
Definir los indicadores y sus definiciones antes de construir el panel.
Para cada indicador: nombre, definición, fórmula, fuente, frecuencia, responsable y meta.
No más de siete indicadores en la primera página.
Organiza el panel: la conclusión arriba, luego la tendencia y después los detalles.
Define los tres filtros más importantes.
El diccionario de indicadores en `Docs/` y el esquema del panel como texto en `Outputs/`.
Correspondencia formal
Redactar un correo o una carta formal breve con una petición concreta.
El asunto lleva la petición.
La primera frase: qué se pide y para cuándo.
Contexto en tres líneas como máximo.
El siguiente paso y el nombre de la persona que lo da.
Español formal, sin cortesías largas y con no más de una petición por mensaje.
Dirección de una reunión
Preparar una reunión y elaborar un acta con decisiones y tareas.
Gestión
Antes
La agenda: tres puntos como máximo y, para cada punto, el propósito (una decisión o información) y el tiempo.
Durante
Para cada punto: la conclusión, la decisión y la tarea con su responsable y fecha de vencimiento.
Después
Un acta de una página en `Docs/` en el plazo de una hora, y las tareas añadidas como filas en el tablero.
Diseño de una encuesta
Una encuesta corta que mide solo lo necesario.
Investigación
Escribe la decisión a la que servirá la encuesta antes de cualquier pregunta.
Diez preguntas como máximo, cada una mide una sola cosa.
Escalas uniformes (de 1 a 5) y una pregunta abierta al final.
Pruébala con tres personas antes de publicarla.
Las preguntas, su escala y el método de análisis en `Outputs/`.
Plan de proyecto
Un plan con hitos, responsables y fechas que se pueda seguir.
El objetivo y el criterio de éxito.
Los hitos (cinco como máximo) con sus fechas.
Para cada hito: las tareas, su responsable y sus dependencias.
Los tres riesgos más importantes y un plan para cada uno.
Ritmo de seguimiento: cuándo se actualiza y quién lo lee.
El plan en `Docs/` y las tareas como filas en el tablero.
Análisis de riesgos
Un registro de riesgos ordenado por probabilidad e impacto.
Reúne los riesgos de todos los roles en una sola sesión.
Para cada riesgo: descripción, probabilidad (1 a 3), impacto (1 a 3) y puntuación.
Para los cinco primeros: la respuesta (evitar, mitigar, transferir, aceptar), su responsable y el indicador de alerta.
Revisa el registro cada dos semanas.
Como tabla ordenada por puntuación.
Análisis DAFO
Fortalezas, debilidades, oportunidades y amenazas basadas en evidencias, no en impresiones.
De tres a cinco elementos en cada cuadrante, y cada elemento tiene su evidencia.
Conéctalos: cómo una fortaleza aprovecha una oportunidad y cómo una debilidad se enfrenta a una amenaza.
Quédate solo con tres prioridades.
Una página en `Outputs/`.
Contenido profesional para LinkedIn
Una publicación profesional que abre con fuerza y termina con una llamada a la acción.
Contenido
La primera línea lleva la idea o la pregunta, porque es lo único que se ve antes de «ver más».
Una historia o un ejemplo concreto.
Tres puntos prácticos como máximo.
Una llamada a la acción al final.
Español formal y claro, párrafos cortos, no más de tres hashtags y ninguna afirmación sin evidencia.
Resumen de un documento
Un resumen exacto que conserva las cifras y las decisiones.
Lee todo el documento antes de escribir ninguna línea.
La conclusión en tres líneas.
Los puntos clave numerados por orden de importancia, con cada cifra o fecha exactamente como aparecía.
Lo que requiere una decisión o una acción va en una sección aparte.
No añadas nada que no esté en el documento.
Un archivo llamado «Resumen de [nombre del documento].md» en `Outputs/`.
Glosario de terminología
Unificar los términos en todos los resultados del proyecto.
Reúne los términos repetidos de la referencia y de los resultados.
Para cada término: la forma aprobada, el equivalente en inglés y los sinónimos prohibidos.
El responsable del rol de referencia aprueba el glosario y cada entregable se revisa con él.
Como tabla ordenada alfabéticamente.
Entrevista con clientes
Una entrevista de descubrimiento que revela la necesidad real.
Ocho preguntas abiertas sobre el pasado («la última vez que…»), no sobre el futuro («¿comprarás?»).
No presentes la solución antes del final de la entrevista.
Registra las citas textualmente.
Tras cinco entrevistas: los patrones recurrentes en tres líneas.
Un archivo por entrevista en `Outputs/Interviews/` y un resumen de los patrones.
Plan de automatización con herramientas sin código

Escribe el procedimiento con sus pasos (la habilidad «Mapeo de procesos»).
Para cada paso: ¿sus entradas son digitales? ¿Su regla es fija? Si es así, es candidato a la automatización.
Dibuja el flujo: el disparador, las condiciones, las acciones y las notificaciones.
Define los datos que no deben salir de las herramientas de la organización.
Prueba con unos pocos casos y luego mide (la habilidad «Medición antes y después»).
La descripción del flujo en `Outputs/` y la tabla de casos en `Data/`.
Cierre semanal
Una ronda semanal que limpia el tablero y mide el avance.
Ejecuta `report` y `export` desde la herramienta.
Mueve las filas aprobadas a `Archive/`.
Revisa las decisiones pendientes de más de 48 horas.
Escribe una circular con la conclusión y las tres prioridades de la semana siguiente.
Un informe en `Docs/Reports/` y una circular en la sección 2 del tablero.
